rationale: B wins because it finds the strongest sell: "The hook is not the feature; it is the session length," then turns the two launches into the cleaner business story, "chess for free, AI conversation for paying subscribers." A is very usable, but "Duolingo adds chess, testing whether its habit machine works beyond language" stretches one course into a platform thesis before the update gives a roadmap. B still needs fact discipline; "free beginner chess course" is an invented adjective doing work it has not earned.
gaps_in_A: "Duolingo bets AI video justifies its priciest tier" overstates the supplied fact. The update says paid Max subscribers, not that Max is the priciest tier or that pricing strategy is disclosed.

"Duolingo is an engagement engine for learning anything" is a sharp thesis, but it outruns the evidence. One free chess course does not prove a cross-category platform strategy without roadmap or prior-course proof.

"live spoken conversation practice is exactly what critics say apps lack" puts extra specificity into the educators' critique. The update only says some educators criticized gamification as shallow learning.
"AI companions moving from chatbots into paid products" is plausible beat framing, but no external trend peg was supplied. It should stay as context, not the headline argument.
gaps_in_B: "putting a free beginner chess course in front of its entire user base" invents "beginner." The course level is not in the update.
"nine minutes at a stretch" and "A nine-minute spoken exchange" overclaim the metric. The update says engagement averaged 9 minutes per session, not that users held one continuous spoken exchange.
"compute-heavy video feature" and "margin risk" may be true, but they are not in the supplied facts. Good question, bad assertion.
"the first public engagement figure for it" is not supported. The update gives an engagement figure; it does not say this is the first public one.
